newsitem.title: USA: Clinton aide subpoenaed on help for Hubbell.
newsitem.headline: Clinton aide subpoenaed on help for Hubbell.

text.p: White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles received a subpoena on Friday to appear before the Whitewater grand jury to answer questions about his efforts to find work for former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell.
"Mr. Bowles has received a subpoena from a federal grand jury in Arkansas, more specifically, from the office of independent counsel Kenneth Starr," a White House official said.
The subpoena requires Bowles to produce documents and appear before the grand jury on a date still to be set.
"He will cooperate fully," the official said.

Hubbell resigned from the Justice Department in 1994 amid controversy over previous conduct as a private citizen and was sent to jail in 1995 after he pleaded guilty to fraudulent billing of clients at the Rose law firm of Little Rock, Arkansas, before he joined the Clinton administration. He and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton were partners at the firm.
The White House disclosed on Tuesday that Bowles and former chief of staff Thomas "Mack" McLarty, had made calls on behalf of Hubbell after he left the Justice Department under a cloud.

Hubbell received payments from the Riady family of Indonesia, which has close ties to President Bill Clinton, for work on a project in China after he resigned. The White House said none of the calls made on Hubbell's behalf involved Lippo, an Indonesian conglomerate run by the Riady family.

The former Clinton associate also got payments from others with ties to Clinton, leading critics to ask if the payments were "hush money" to keep him from telling what he knew about the Whitewater case, a tangled web of financial, legal and ethical questions that have dogged Clinton and his wife since Clinton's 1992 campaign for the presidency.
Hubbell has denied he is withholding information that would be damaging to the president and his wife.
Clinton defended Bowles and McLarty, saying on Thursday he did not think it was wrong for two senior officials to try to find work for Hubbell.

"I do not believe they (the calls) were improper. From what I know about them, they were just people who were mainly concerned that a man with four children was out of work and they were trying to help him for no other reason than just out of human compassion," Clinton said.

"Let me remind you of the critical fact that at the time that was done (the telephone calls for Hubbell), no one had any idea what the nature of the allegations was against Mr. Hubbell or whether they were true," Clinton said.
